findings.title: baseline_delayed_horizon_and_protective_choice
findings.claim: The later abode is the controlling horizon of the historical comparison: reason delays judgment, compares whole sequences, and chooses present protection by the final rather than immediate state. This attributed reading is held alongside the baseline, not as a replacement for the ayah's ordinary wording.
findings.mechanism: The two qabl-phrases (12:109:4:1, 12:109:22:1) fold prior horizons around the audience; yanẓurū and ʿāqibah (12:109:16:2, 12:109:19:1) make their outcomes inspectable, while dār al-ākhirah and khayrun (12:109:23:3, 12:109:24:2, 12:109:25:1) supply the later comparison. Ittaqaw and taʿqilūna (12:109:27:1, 12:109:29:1) connect that horizon to present guarded conduct and reasoning. The nominated general-barrier branch is excluded because the actual verb is Form VIII self-guarding. The HFT's practical protective-posture role is retained through self-guarding under the later-horizon comparison; only the external-barrier account is excluded.
findings.reader_payoff: The historical warning and the afterlife statement can be read as one temporal comparison: earlier outcomes inform a reasoned present posture toward a later abode. This adds a horizon to the reward clause without making the earlier warning disappear.
findings.containment: Keep the baseline before-reading visible: “The afterlife clause is a conventional reward appended to a warning about old peoples.” The ordinary warning, the better later abode, and the guarded beneficiaries all remain intact. The afterlife-horizon reading adds how the historical sequences inform the present; it does not replace the reward clause. The dār-to-inhabitant link is explicitly metonymic and attributed, and the general-barrier branch is excluded because the actual carrier is reflexive Form VIII self-guarding.
